content:
Hi,

I am a master student, and in the development of my master thesis I have been using the tactic mvcgen. I would like to cite an academic reference for it. Is there a paper about the idea behind the tool? @Sebastian Graf Thank you in advance for your time.

Hi, there is no academic reference for the current approach implemented in mvcgen, I'm afraid. You could cite the reference manual if you want.

The closest to a published description of the meta theory of mvcgen is that of Loom: #General announcements > Loom: framework for Multi Modal program verifiers in Lean @ 💬 . Both approaches were developed independently, though, and there isn't much focus on VC generation. I'm working with the author @Vladimir Gladstein on a new version of mvcgen that builds on a unified meta theory that combines the strengths of both and that will underpin Loom 2.0 as well.
Thank you very much for the quick answer, I think I will then cite the reference manual. Excited to see what is to come!

@Sebastian Graf Do you have a clear comparison with the Dijkstra monad approach? I understand both Loom and mcvgen use special cases of DM that are easier to implement/more practical to use. Is that a fair understanding? Will you use the same methodology for Loom 2?

Hmm, I would say that the approach of both Loom and mvcgen is more general than Dijkstra monads. Dijkstra monads don't allow the user to specify fine-grained exception conditions, for example; it's either partial or total correctness. See the section on Exceptions in the tutorial. Using mvcgen, one can specify and prove that if an exception is thrown in the following program, then the resource limit state.limit has been reached in the internal state (state.counter = state.limit):

theorem mkFreshN_spec (n : Nat) :
    ⦃⌜True⌝⦄
    mkFreshN n
    ⦃post⟨fun r => ⌜r.Nodup⌝,
          fun _msg state => ⌜state.counter = state.limit⌝⟩⦄

On the other hand, the appeal of Dijsktra monads is to compute the weakest precondition of a program while elaborating it and attach it intrinsically to its type. Perfect fit for F*, but that's not necessary in Lean where we compute the weakest precondition extrinsically.

The approach shares with Dijkstra monads the translation of a Monad stack M into a corresponding assertion language L, and a translation from monadic programs x : m α into predicate transformers over L. However, Dijkstra monads is IMO overinterpreting this connection, wanting it to be more rigid than necessary (even a monad morphism). By contrast, next Std.Do/Loom 2.0 will come with a meta theory that can be instantiated even with deep embeddings such as operational semantics, and there isn't even a Monad that you can talk about in that scenario. Yet you will be able to run mvcgen to generate VCs. It's just VC generation taken to its most general and reusable form.

What's the lesson from this? The current categorical frameworks are not strong enough (?). You are building something practical and someone in the future might come up with a more principled (categorical) solution? Which would be an entirely reasonable approach. :-)

So the new, general notion of "a program's weakest precondition" is

structure PredTrans (Pred : Type u) (EPred : Type v) (α : Type w) where
  /-- Apply the predicate transformer to a postcondition and exception postcondition. -/
  apply : (α → Pred) → EPred → Pred

class WP (α : Type u) (ρ : outParam (Type v)) (Pred : outParam (Type w))
    (EPred : outParam (Type w')) [CompleteLattice Pred] [CompleteLattice EPred] where
  /-- The weakest precondition transformer for a program `α` with value `ρ`. -/
  trans : α → PredTrans Pred EPred ρ
  /-- Monotonicity: weaker postconditions yield weaker preconditions. -/
  trans_monotone (x : α) : trans x |>.monotone

(Example hypothetical instance for PCF: WP PCF.Expr PCF.Value (PCF.State -> Prop) Unit.)

I don't know what categorical abstraction is worth recognizing here and what it will buy you in terms of generalization to other, exciting use cases.

Do you have a class of programming features in mind that you want to support?
PCF has higher-order features, so that may bring you into iris like logics.
Yes, compatibility with iris-lean is in scope. However, I've heard that it's not very useful to generate VCs for separation logics because you'll need to specify frames manually
